chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from Abu Abdullah Al-Abdullah, from Abu Abdullah Al-Jamourani, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Al-Mu'min, from Is'haq ibn 'Ammar, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): 'Is the hadith that people narrate true, that a man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and complained to him of need/poverty, so he ordered him to marry, and he did? Then he came to him and complained to him of need, so he ordered him to marry, until he ordered him three times?'
So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: '[Yes]' it is true. Then he said: 'Sustenance is with the women and the dependents.'
ai.seo_question: Does marriage increase one's sustenance according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) validates the well-known tradition that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) advised a man struggling with poverty to marry, doing so three times to emphasize its importance. The Imam elucidates the theological principle that sustenance (*rizq*) is intrinsically linked to family life, suggesting that the responsibilities of providing for women and dependents serve as a catalyst for divine provision rather than a burden. This reflects the Shia scholarly view that marriage is not merely a social contract but a spiritual mechanism for increasing one's share of worldly and spiritual blessings.
